content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain oatmeal is a blend of whole oat flakes, wheat, barley, rye and other grains. The product is rich in complex carbohydrates, fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals, making it a nutritious and filling breakfast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oatmeal contains beta‑glucans – soluble fiber that helps lower cholesterol levels.
A multigrain mix provides a broader spectrum of nutrients compared with plain oats.
Oat flakes can be used not only in hot porridge but also in cold dishes, smoothies and baked goods.
Heat processing retains most B‑vitamins, while some vitamin C is lost.
Oatmeal has long been considered a "champion's breakfast" because of its sustained energy release.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Beta‑glucans help reduce LDL‑cholesterol, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: Complex carbs and soluble fiber slow glucose absorption, preventing sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Improves digestion
items.content: Fiber promotes intestinal motility and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals for bone health
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and iron contribute to strong bones and muscle function.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or other grains in the blend.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Multigrain oatmeal often contains traces of gluten from wheat, barley or rye, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High glycemic index with added sugar
items.content: Adding large amounts of sugar or honey to the prepared porridge can raise its glycemic index.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook oatmeal in water or milk for 5‑10 minutes, then add fruit, nuts, honey or spices to taste. It can also be prepared as cold "overnight oats" by mixing with yogurt and refrigerating overnight.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place, tightly sealed. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and use within 3‑4 months. Discard if you notice moldy or rancid odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw vegetables are fresh, unprocessed vegetables that have not undergone any heat treatment. They retain the maximum amount of vitamins, minerals, and enzymes characteristic of each type. The product is intended for consumption in its natural state, in salads, smoothies, or as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Raw vegetables contain over 90 % water, making them a low‑calorie food.
Most vitamin C is destroyed by heating, so it remains fully intact when eaten raw.
The variety of colors in vegetables is due to different phytochemical compounds that are beneficial for health.
Raw vegetables are a staple in Mediterranean and Asian culinary traditions.
Some vegetables, such as broccoli and cauliflower, contain glucoraphanin, which forms health‑promoting sulforaphane when cut.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Raw vegetables are an excellent source of vitamins A, C, K and B‑complex, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: The high water and fiber content makes them ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as carotenoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium, magnesium, and balanced sodium help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw vegetables can be contaminated with bacteria (e.g., E. coli) or parasites, so they should be washed thoroughly.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: For some people, the high fiber content may cause gas and bloating.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables such as celery.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts of kale or spinach can affect anticoagulant therapy due to high vitamin K levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw vegetables can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, blended into smoothies, used in wraps, or as a base for dips. They can also be lightly marinated in lemon juice and olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw vegetables in the refrigerator in perforated bags or a ventilated container. Most vegetables stay fresh for 5‑7 days. Rinse them thoroughly under running water before consumption.

rice-brown-and-wild-cooked-fat-added.title: Rice, brown and wild, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown and wild rice are whole grains that retain the bran and germ, making them rich in fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals. When cooked with added fat (oil, butter, or other fats) the energy density increases and the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins improves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild rice (Zizania) is not a true rice but a grass species, yet it is marketed as rice because of its similar flavor and texture.
Brown rice keeps the bran layer, giving it a lower glycemic index than white rice.
Wild rice contains higher levels of antioxidants compared with most common rice varieties.
Cooking rice with a small amount of fat enhances mouthfeel and makes the dish more satiating.
In Japan, wild rice is traditionally used in festive dishes and sushi.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nervous system health, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is important for protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Beneficial fats and antioxidants help lower LDL cholesterol and protect blood vessels.

items.title: Energy‑dense
items.content: Added fat raises the calorie content, providing a good energy source for active individuals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the added fat, the dish can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Arsenic presence
items.content: Brown rice can accumulate trace amounts of arsenic from soil; rinsing thoroughly and rotating with other grains reduces exposure.

items.title: Fat allergies
items.content: People with allergies to specific oils should choose alternative fats that do not trigger reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish, add it to salads, soups, or pilafs. Use 1–2 tablespoons of oil, butter, or another fat during cooking to enhance flavor and nutrient absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with added fat should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 3–4 days.

rice-white-with-vegetables-soy-based-sau.title: White Rice with Vegetables and Soy Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This is a ready‑to‑eat dish of boiled white rice mixed with a variety of vegetables (carrot, peas, corn) and a soy‑based sauce. A small amount of vegetable fat is added to enhance flavor and increase the energy value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food in many Asian countries.
Soy sauce was invented in China more than 2,500 years ago.
Vegetables are usually steamed to preserve maximum vitamins.
Adding a little fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
The dish is convenient to store and reheat in a microwave.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of carbohydrates, while the added fat raises the caloric content, useful for higher energy needs.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables supply vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, and soy sauce contributes iron and magnesium.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Soy sauce contains soy protein, complementing the amino acid profile of rice.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables promotes normal bowel function.

items.title: Flavor enhancement with less salt
items.content: Soy sauce adds umami, allowing a reduction in added salt.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in sodium; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added fat increases overall calories, so portion control is important.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish can be enjoyed as a standalone meal or as a side. It reheats well in the microwave or on a skillet. Add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a dash of hot sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though the rice texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain Greek yogurt with no added sugar is a thick, creamy dairy product made by double‑straining regular yogurt. It contains a higher protein content and fewer carbohydrates than traditional yogurt, with a mildly tangy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt originates from Greece, where it is known as “straggini”.
Double‑straining removes most of the whey, giving the product its dense texture.
Because of its low sugar content, it is popular in diet and keto plans.
It is often served with nuts, berries or honey, but is also enjoyed plain as a protein source.
In some countries Greek yogurt is classified as a distinct dairy product rather than a yogurt variant.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: A 200 ml serving provides about 10–12 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: No added sugar makes it suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Contains live cultures such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium that support gut health.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Like other dairy products, it is a good source of calcium for bone health and is often fortified with vitamin D.

items.title: Low fat (in non‑fat versions)
items.content: Non‑fat Greek yogurt contains minimal saturated fat, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, a small amount remains.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Greek yogurt.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add a pinch of salt for flavor; check labels if you watch sodium intake.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature can erode tooth enamel with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plain Greek yogurt can be eaten on its own, blended into smoothies, used as a base for sauces, dressings, desserts, or in baking as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
